metadata.title: Why Musk's SpaceX control is an 'all-out assault' on US market integrity

content.text:
Yale School of Management executive fellow and "Picking Presidents" author, Gautam Mukunda, sits down with Yahoo Finance's Julie Hyman to explain how Elon Musk's 85% voting share at SpaceX (SPAX.PVT) poses a grave threat to US capital markets.
There has been a lot of talk about this 85% voting share and the control that Musk has over this company. What are the specific risks in this kind of structure?
There are two types of risks and let's sort of set them out, right? So one is the normal risk that we worry about where there are going to be exploitations of minority shareholders or he's going to use this to favor himself, you know, like you're already hearing rumors about plans to merge Tesla and SpaceX into some kind of, you know, Musk Musk conglomerate.
I think the other and more profound set of risks and the ones that I think if I were part of this, I would be much more worried about, is just that all of these things that they're getting, all these special privileges, all these institutional safeguards, they are all designed to make Elon Musk sort of someone who cannot even be contradicted within SpaceX, right? Who can govern it with by his whim, who doesn't need to justify himself, does not need to argue his own positions, and all anyone can do is say yes.
No matter how brilliant you think Elon Musk is, in the entire history of humanity, there has never lived a leader who was better off when he didn't have anyone around him or she didn't have anyone around her who could say, hey, I'm not sure this is a great idea. Let's see if we can do better.
Do you think that there are also sort of systemic risks here, um, that this is going to become even more common if indeed the SpaceX one goes off without a hitch?
There absolutely are. And I I think it's really clear to sort of lay out what's happening here. This is an this is a all-out assault on the integrity of American capital markets. The depth and efficiency and fairness of American capital markets has been one of the basic foundations of American economic success. It is one of the things that sets us apart from everyone else. Just the fact that if you engaged in improper behaviors, insider trading, things like that, the SEC would come after you.
I remember when Raj Rajaratnam was put in prison for insider trading, right? I was at a HBS faculty meeting and one of my colleagues who was from Italy, you know, stuck his hand up and said, you guys don't understand how special this is. You just put a billionaire in prison and in the rest of the world, even in Western Europe, that doesn't happen. So what we're seeing here is the characteristics that made those markets special, that made people think they were fair, that made people think they were protected, are being broken in order to curry favor with SpaceX and with Elon Musk. And as we already saw with his massive pay packages at Tesla, what Musk does, other people facing the same temptations and the same pressures and the same problems, they'll go in the same direction.
We're seeing the SEC being completely defanged by the Trump administration. The Justice department where has essentially stopped prosecuting white collar crimes under this administration. You're seeing insider trading by government in by government insiders where suspicious time trades with regard to the war in Iran or everything else seem to happen now on a routine basis. So, is SpaceX the only problem? No, of course not. But is SpaceX one of a number of different assaults on the on on the capital markets, all of which have the same root, right? They are designed to favor the powerful and the influential and the well-connected over sort of the the the retail investor or the a person who just doesn't have access to the upper levels of the government. The SpaceX IPO could not have been more clearly defined, designed to be a wealth transfer from everyday investors to SpaceX insiders. That is not how the capital markets were supposed to work.
